title: Research
text:
LETR Lab
    Research
    We explore the processes underlying learning across contexts and for all learners — examining individual differences in cognition, language, and motivation.
  




  Current Focus
  New Projects
  Two new projects launching in the coming year bring eye-tracking and multimodal AI into the lab's research program.

  

    
      👁️
      Patricia Miller Fund
      Profiling Readers with Eye Tracking
      
        Readers differ meaningfully in the cognitive, motivational, and knowledge-based resources they bring to a text — yet prior research on reader profiles has relied almost entirely on self-report and performance measures, leaving eye movement data largely absent. This project integrates gaze behavior into a person-centered investigation of reading comprehension, comparing neurotypical readers and readers on the autism spectrum. Using the Microsoft HoloLens with VeYezer Graph eye tracking software, participants can move freely during reading — overcoming a key limitation of traditional static trackers that are especially burdensome for individuals with ASD. The study examines fixations, regressions, span of recognition, and fixation duration alongside background knowledge, prior interest, and engagement, asking whether existing reader profiles hold, require refinement, or differ across populations.
      
    

    
      🤝
      Ken Fong Translational Research Award
      Vision[AI]ry: Emotion & Attention Analytics for Education
      
        Students' emotional states directly shape learning — yet instructors in online environments lack the moment-to-moment visibility needed to detect confusion, frustration, or disengagement. In collaboration with Dr. Sanchita Ghose (Computer Engineering, AI-LAMP Lab), this project develops Vision[AI]ry, a multimodal platform that fuses facial expression analysis, vocal emotion recognition, and gaze-based attention tracking into real-time engagement scores. The system integrates three components — facial landmark detection via CNN, audio Mel-spectrogram analysis, and posture-based attention tracking — through a novel multimodal fusion algorithm deployed on edge computing hardware with low latency. The psychological component focuses on validating Vision[AI]ry against established self-report measures of learning-relevant affect (confusion, frustration, boredom, engaged concentration), with classroom deployment planned in online psychology and engineering courses. The platform will be released as open-source software for educational institutions.
      
    

  

  

  Ongoing Work
  Other Research Areas
  Alongside the new projects, the lab continues work in three areas developed over the past several years.

  

    
      📖
      Reading Across Mediums
      
        Does reading format — print, digital screen, or audio — shape what readers take away from a text? This line of work examines comprehension, engagement, and metacognition across formats, with completed studies on audiobook vs. print comprehension and multiple digital source use.
      
    

    
      🧠
      Knowledge, Beliefs & Reasoning
      
        How and why do people revise — or resist revising — their beliefs about controversial scientific topics? This work investigates knowledge updating, argumentative writing, and the interplay between evidence, emotion, and prior beliefs, using Bayesian network modeling and qualitative methods.
      
    

    
      🌱
      Mental Health in Academia
      
        Funded by an American Psychological Foundation (APF) Grant, this project examines the mental health and well-being of early career academics, investigating systemic, relational, and individual factors that shape stress, belonging, and career sustainability.
      
    

  

  

  Methods
  How We Work
  We use a range of quantitative and qualitative methods depending on the question.

  
    
      📊
      Quantitative Methods
      Survey methods, experimental designs, psychometric modeling, Bayesian network analysis, and statistical approaches appropriate to the research question.
    
    
      🔍
      Qualitative Methods
      Think-aloud protocols, interviews, and discourse analysis to examine the processes underlying learning, argumentation, and belief revision.
    
    
      📝
      Mixed Methods
      Many projects combine quantitative and qualitative approaches to capture both the breadth and depth of learning phenomena.
    
  

  

  Join the Lab
  Working with Students
  I'm always excited to work with students who are genuinely curious about the world and eager to ask meaningful questions. More than prior experience, I value intellectual curiosity, intrinsic motivation, and a willingness to engage with complex, open-ended problems where the answers are not immediately obvious.
  Research often begins with big ideas. But meaningful progress comes from carefully breaking those ideas into questions that can be studied systematically. I'm looking for students who enjoy thinking deeply, discussing ideas, and are equally willing to put in the sustained effort required to design studies, analyze data, and refine their thinking. If you enjoy learning, embrace ambiguity, and are excited by the challenge of turning difficult questions into rigorous research, I'd love to hear from you.

        We welcome inquiries from researchers, practitioners, and students interested in our work.

title: R Basics for Psychological Research
text:
Step 1: Load Libraries
Use install.packages("psych") once if you have not installed it yet. Then load it each session:

library(psych)   # for the describe() function

A library (package) is a collection of pre-written functions that extend base R. Load with library() at the top of every script.

title: R Basics for Psychological Research
text:
Step 2: Import the Dataset

df <- read.csv("psych_study_data.csv")
head(df)     # first 6 rows

4          4         7.3         7.1            43       62.5

text:

3a. Mean and Standard Deviation (base R)

mean(df$exam_score)

mean(df$study_hours)

[1] 10.21197


A larger SD indicates more variability around the mean; a smaller SD means scores cluster tightly.


3b. Rich Descriptives with psych::describe()

# Drop column 1 (student_id) before describing

title: R Basics for Psychological Research
text:
Step 4: Correlation with cor.test()
cor.test() returns Pearson r and tests whether it differs significantly from zero.

Study Hours and Exam Score

cor.test(df$study_hours, df$exam_score)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  df$study_hours and df$exam_score
t = 10.014, df = 148, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.5291560 0.7222259
sample estimates:
     cor 
0.635523 




Anxiety Score and Exam Score

cor.test(df$anxiety_score, df$exam_score)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  df$anxiety_score and df$exam_score
t = -3.9774, df = 148, p-value = 0.0001087
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.4486713 -0.1583807
sample estimates:
       cor 
-0.3107545 




Sleep Hours and Exam Score

cor.test(df$sleep_hours, df$exam_score)


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  df$sleep_hours and df$exam_score
t = 3.2379, df = 148, p-value = 0.001486
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.1011083 0.4009372
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.2572022 


Reading the output: - cor: Pearson r (range -1 to +1) - t: test statistic - df: degrees of freedom (n - 2) - p-value: probability of this result if the true r = 0 - 95 percent confidence interval: plausible range for the true r
Effect size convention (Cohen, 1988): |r| < .10 = negligible; .10-.29 = small; .30-.49 = moderate; >= .50 = large.

title: R Basics for Psychological Research
text:
Step 5: Multiple Regression
Multiple regression estimates how several predictors jointly explain an outcome and the unique contribution of each predictor controlling for the others.

model <- lm(exam_score ~ study_hours + sleep_hours + anxiety_score, data = df)
summary(model)


Call:
lm(formula = exam_score ~ study_hours + sleep_hours + anxiety_score, 
    data = df)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-17.801  -5.827  -0.101   5.199  17.417 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   36.66864    5.35935   6.842 2.00e-10 ***
study_hours    4.19120    0.33653  12.454  < 2e-16 ***
sleep_hours    2.82049    0.51175   5.511 1.57e-07 ***
anxiety_score -0.36945    0.06265  -5.897 2.47e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 7.805 on 146 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.5917,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5833 
F-statistic: 70.53 on 3 and 146 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Reading the output:
Coefficients table: - Estimate: regression slope (B) - Std. Error: precision of the estimate - t value: test statistic (H0: B = 0) - Pr(>|t|): p-value; *** <= .001, ** <= .01, * <= .05
Model fit: - Multiple R-squared: proportion of variance in exam score explained by all predictors combined - Adjusted R-squared: R-squared penalized for number of predictors (preferred for comparisons) - F-statistic: tests whether the overall model is significant
Interpreting a slope: for every one-unit increase in a predictor, exam score changes by B points holding all other predictors constant.

title: Introduction to R
text:
PSY 771 · ANOVA and Experimental Design
    
    Getting started with R: objects, data types, descriptive statistics, and basic plotting.

title: Introduction to R
text:
What is R?
R is a free, open-source programming language and environment designed for statistical computing and graphics. It is widely used in psychology, education, biology, economics, and virtually every other field that involves data.
Unlike point-and-click software such as SPSS, R is a scripting language — you write code that tells R exactly what to do, step by step. This takes a little more effort to learn at first, but it pays off quickly: your analyses are reproducible, flexible, and well-documented.






NoteWhy code instead of click?



A script is a permanent record of every decision you made in your analysis. When you (or a reviewer) want to know exactly what you did — and in what order — the script tells you. Point-and-click software does not.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Why R?

Free and open source. R costs nothing and runs on Mac, Windows, and Linux.
Reproducible. Your entire analysis lives in a script you can re-run, share, or modify.
Publication quality. R produces clean, customizable figures ready for journals and presentations.
Community. Thousands of user-contributed packages extend R’s capabilities. Whatever analysis you need, there is almost certainly a package for it.
Industry and academia. R is used in research labs, tech companies, public health agencies, and psychology departments worldwide. Learning it now is a career-long investment.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Downloading R and RStudio
You need two things: R (the language) and RStudio (the editor that makes R easier to use). Think of R as the engine and RStudio as the dashboard.

Download R from cran.r-project.org

Choose your operating system (Mac or Windows)
Install the most recent version

Download RStudio Desktop (free) from posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop

Install after R is installed
Always open RStudio, not R directly


When RStudio opens you will see four panes:







Pane
What it does




Source (top-left)
Where you write and save scripts


Console (bottom-left)
Where R runs code and shows output


Environment (top-right)
Lists objects currently in memory


Files / Plots / Help (bottom-right)
Browse files, see plots, read documentation

title: Introduction to R
text:
R as a Calculator
At its simplest, R is a very powerful calculator. Type an expression in the Console and press Enter:
1 + 1
[1] 2
The [1] simply means “this is the first element of the result.” You will see it with every output.
More examples:
10 - 3      # subtraction
4 * 5       # multiplication
20 / 4      # division
2 ^ 8       # exponentiation (2 to the power of 8)
sqrt(144)   # square root
log(100)    # natural log






TipComments with #



Anything after a # on a line is a comment. R ignores it when running the code. Use comments generously to explain what your code does — your future self will thank you.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Objects
In R, you save values by assigning them to objects. Use <- (the assignment arrow) to create an object:
X <- 8
Now X holds the value 8. Type X and press Enter to see it:
X
[1] 8
You can do arithmetic with objects:
X + 2       # 10
X * X       # 64
sqrt(X)     # 2.828...

Vectors
A vector is a sequence of values. Create one with c() (short for “combine”):
Y <- c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
Y
[1] 1 2 3 4 5
Arithmetic on a vector applies to every element:
Y * 2       # [1]  2  4  6  8 10
Y + 10      # [1] 11 12 13 14 15


Matrices
A matrix is a two-dimensional array of values. Create one with matrix():
Z <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3, ncol = 3)
Z
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    4    7
[2,]    2    5    8
[3,]    3    6    9
The numbers fill in column by column by default.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data Frames and Classes
Real data is usually stored in a data frame — a table with rows (observations) and columns (variables). R comes with several built-in datasets for practice.
mtcars is a classic: 32 cars, 11 variables including miles per gallon, cylinders, horsepower, and weight.
head(mtcars)      # first 6 rows
Access a single column with $:
mtcars$cyl        # the cylinder variable
 [1] 6 6 4 6 8 6 8 4 4 6 6 8 8 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 4 8 8 8 8 4 4 4 8 6 8 4

Checking Classes
Every object in R has a class — a label that tells R (and you) what type of thing it is:
class(mtcars)        # "data.frame"
class(mtcars$cyl)    # "numeric"
class("hello")       # "character"
class(TRUE)          # "logical"
The class determines which functions can be applied. Most errors in R trace back to a class mismatch — feeding a character vector to a function that expects numbers, for example.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Descriptive Statistics
Once data is loaded, computing summary statistics is straightforward. The attach() function lets you refer to a dataset’s columns by name without the $:
attach(mtcars)

mean(mpg)     # mean
sd(mpg)       # standard deviation
var(mpg)      # variance
max(mpg)      # maximum
min(mpg)      # minimum
range(mpg)    # minimum and maximum together






WarningUse attach() carefully



attach() makes column names available globally, which is convenient but can cause confusion if two datasets share column names. For complex scripts, prefer dataset$variable notation or use the with() function.



Correlations
cor(mpg, hp)           # correlation between mpg and horsepower
cor(mtcars)            # full correlation matrix for all variables


summary() — your best friend
summary() gives you a five-number summary plus the mean for every numeric column:
summary(mtcars)
      mpg             cyl             disp             hp
 Min.   :10.40   Min.   :4.000   Min.   : 71.1   Min.   : 52.0
 1st Qu.:15.43   1st Qu.:4.000   1st Qu.:120.8   1st Qu.: 96.5
 Median :19.20   Median :6.000   Median :196.3   Median :123.0
 Mean   :20.09   Mean   :6.188   Mean   :230.7   Mean   :146.7
 3rd Qu.:22.80   3rd Qu.:8.000   3rd Qu.:326.0   3rd Qu.:180.0
 Max.   :33.90   Max.   :8.000   Max.   :472.0   Max.   :335.0

title: Introduction to R
text:
Basic Plots
R produces publication-quality graphics. The base graphics functions are quick to use and good for exploration.

Histogram
Visualize the distribution of a single variable:
hist(mpg,
     main  = "Distribution of Miles per Gallon",
     xlab  = "MPG",
     col   = "steelblue",
     border = "white")
Key arguments:



Argument
What it does




main
Plot title


xlab
x-axis label


col
Bar fill color


breaks
Number of bins (optional)





Boxplot
Visualize the distribution of a variable across groups:
boxplot(mpg ~ cyl,
        data = mtcars,
        main = "MPG by Number of Cylinders",
        xlab = "Cylinders",
        ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
        col  = c("steelblue", "tomato", "seagreen"))
The ~ (tilde) reads as “by” — MPG by cylinders.


Scatterplot
Visualize the relationship between two numeric variables:
plot(hp, mpg,
     main = "Horsepower vs. MPG",
     xlab = "Horsepower",
     ylab = "Miles per Gallon",
     pch  = 19,
     col  = "steelblue")
pch = 19 gives you solid circles. Try values 1–25 to see different point shapes.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Getting Help
When you are unsure how a function works, use the ? operator:
?mean
?hist
?lm
The Help pane on the bottom-right will show the function’s documentation: what it does, what arguments it accepts, and examples.
You can also search by keyword:
??regression      # searches all documentation for "regression"

title: Introduction to R
text:
Next Steps
You now have the foundations: objects, data frames, classes, descriptive statistics, and basic plots. The rest of the course builds on these — each week’s R script will introduce the functions needed for the statistical model we cover that week.
Continue with the PSY 371 R Basics page for additional exercises including importing data from CSV and working with real datasets.
